lines: Stereo multimode filter offering 35 filter modes and bypass, with zero-delay feedback topologies, 4x oversampled drive, and a jack for every control
Sets the gain into the filter, 0 to 100%, which is nothing at the bottom and 40dB at the top; the harder it is driven the more it soft-clips and the less the resonance peaks
Attenuates and inverts the voltage at the DRIVE jack, -100% to +100%; at either end 10V covers the whole travel of the drive knob
Sets the cutoff frequency, 20Hz to 20000Hz
Attenuates and inverts the voltage at the FREQ jack, -100% to +100%; at either end 10V covers the whole travel of the frequency knob
Sets the resonance, 0 to 100%, raising a peak in the response at the cutoff frequency
Attenuates and inverts the voltage at the RES jack, -100% to +100%; at either end 10V covers the whole travel of the resonance knob
Blends the dry input with the filtered signal, 0 to 100% filtered, despite the manual describing this knob as a modulation rate
Adds to the drive knob, where 10V covers its whole travel once the drive attenuverter is open
Adds to the frequency knob, where 10V covers its whole travel once the frequency attenuverter is open, which puts the cutoff within a third of a semitone of a volt per octave
Adds to the resonance knob, where 10V covers its whole travel once the resonance attenuverter is open
Moves the filter mode on from the one chosen on the display, by three and a half modes per volt, and holds at the last of the 36 beyond that
Adds to the MIX knob, where 10V covers the whole of that knob's travel
The left audio input into the filter
The right audio input into the filter
The left output, carrying dry and filtered signal in the proportion set by MIX
The right output, carrying dry and filtered signal in the proportion set by MIX
Note — clicking the mode display opens the 36 modes: bypass, two Sallen-Key, eight state variable, sixteen transistor ladder, a diode ladder, three dual resonator, two comb, FM, RM and a bitcrusher
Note — each filter mode is named with its slope in dB per octave, and two modes of the same slope sound alike until the resonance is raised
Note — a pole gives a slope of 6dB per octave, so a mode named 24 is a four-pole filter
Note — the two comb modes feed a delayed copy of the signal back on itself, which is the mechanism behind chorus, phasing and flanging
Note — the FM mode varies the frequency of the input with a sine wave
Note — the RM mode varies the amplitude of the input with a sine wave
Note — the bitcrusher mode reduces the sample rate and the bit depth of the input
Note — the module is polyphonic and takes its channel count from whichever audio input carries more channels
Blamsoft-XFXF35.notes: Blamsoft publish no source; everything here was read out of the installed 2.0.2 binary. The two unlabelled jacks in the MIX row are settled by the panel's own connector artwork, which draws a line from the left jack up to the mode display and from the right jack across to the MIX knob, and by the disassembly: XFXFilterModule::process reads input 3 as mode = display mode + int(v*3.5 + 0.5) clamped to 0-35, and input 4 as mix = knob + 0.1v clamped to 0-1. The frequency jack is tagged pitch: the cutoff runs 20Hz to 20000Hz over the knob's full travel and 10V covers that travel with the attenuverter open, which is 9.97 octaves for 10V, so it tracks a volt per octave to within a third of a semitone over the full 10V. The manual's MIX paragraph is copied verbatim from the XFX Reverb manual and describes an LFO; the code blends dry input against filtered output. The manual also describes comb, FM, RM and bitcrusher modes as non-traditional additions, and all four are present in this build. The widget adds no context menu of its own; the filter-mode submenus in the binary (Sallen-Key, State Variable, Ladder, Dual Resonator, Comb) belong to the mode display's own menu, which the note above says is opened by clicking the display. The maker's PDF manual was read on this pass with pypdf; it supplied the slope-per-pole convention and the account of the comb, FM, RM and bitcrusher modes, which it groups as non-traditional. The 36 mode names are a pointer table in the binary and all 36 are present, FM and RM included; a plain strings pass misses those two because they are under four characters long.
